metadata.subtitle: What a Skill Actually Is

beats.narration_text: Call something a case-brief skill and it sounds like Claude studied law. Wrong branch. It was handed a text file to read before it starts. So what is actually inside that file?

What is a skill?

beats.narration_text: Here is what people project onto that name. They hear 'case-brief skill' and read it as new knowledge — as if Claude went off, studied case law, and came back smarter than it was before. That is the natural read. It is also the wrong one.

The proof is subtractive. Delete the skill's folder and nothing in the model shifts — no case law falls out, because none went in. The only thing that disappears is the routine. That tells you where the machinery actually lives: outside the model, in text on disk.

Here is what a skill actually is. One file. Case-brief is a folder wrapped around a single SKILL.md — plain-language instructions for turning case facts into a structured brief. They chose Markdown a person can read and edit over compiled logic Claude had to be trained on. That priority is the whole design: the routine has to be legible to the human who wrote it.

The execution is boring on purpose. Claude reads the file top to bottom and runs the steps in the order they appear. No branching, no cleverness — unless the file itself says branch. They optimized for predictability at the expense of adaptivity, and that is the whole reason the outputs come out the same shape each run.

So a skill is a specification, not a new power. This works if you value repeatability: every brief lands with the same four sections — facts, issue, rule, conclusion. It fails the moment the case falls outside what the file describes. Then Claude is off the map, doing whatever the general model would have done anyway.

Which is why case-brief never taught Claude how to read case law. The trick is guarantee, not knowledge. Every run reads the same file, executes the same steps, produces the same document shape. What you are actually buying is invariance — the confidence that the brief you get today matches the brief you'll get tomorrow.

beats.narration_text: And that has a cost on both ends. A clean brief does not prove Claude understood the case — the file can be followed to the letter on facts the model never really grasped. A messy brief does not prove the skill is broken — the case may just not fit the structure the file assumes. The output tells you the routine ran; it does not tell you the routine matched the problem.
A skill doesn't teach Claude how to read a case — it's a file of steps Claude reads before it starts, so every brief comes out with the same structure, every time.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I produce a specific kind of document the same way every time — reports, briefs, meeting notes, whatever it is for me. Write me a SKILL.md for one of them: plain language, ordered steps a model could follow top to bottom without branching. Then read it back to me and walk me through exactly what you would do, step by step, before you actually do it — so I can see which steps are on the page and which ones I was quietly relying on being in my head. Go deeper: run the same skill against a case that almost fits but not quite. Where does the file's structure force the wrong shape, and what would you have to add to the SKILL.md to catch that case without breaking the easy ones?
